extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political theory, comparative government, and American political history
extracted.subtask_description: Close analytic account of the alleged and actual faults of democratic government, with emphasis on the United States — identifying tendencies, structural causes, and concrete manifestations of those faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caesarism / military despotism risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Caesarism is the last danger likely to menace America; no nation is civil order more stable, none more averse to the military spirit, and no political system would offer a greater resistance to an attempt to create a standing army or centralize the administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why military despotism is unlikely in the U.S.: disbandment of victorious Civil War armies (Appomattox), the social reintegration of generals (Grant, Sherman, Sheridan), and institutional resistance. Use as a criterion: assess stability of civil order, public aversion to military spirit, and institutional barriers to standing armies/centralized military power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jealousy of greatness / desire to level down
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy has a tendency to dislike and resent outward manifestations of social superiority — politicians adopt modest, Cincinnatus-like poses, and outward luxury may be criticized as unfit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manifestations include public figures staging modest homes/farm images, avoidance of ostentation during campaigns, and political theatre that emphasizes equality. Counter-evidence: wealthy Americans still publicly display great wealth (e.g., Fifth Avenue, Newport); intellectual eminence is admired. Use as a criterion to judge how social superiority is received and whether public attitudes penalize or tolerate conspicuous wealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tyranny of the majority
rubrics_metrics.description: The fear that majorities will oppress minorities through compulsive legislation is over-stated in the U.S.; press is free, religious practices are untouched, and widespread compulsory abuses are limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate instances where majorities might tax or legislate against the rich or other groups (temptation exists) but note constitutional and popular restraints. Consider party composition (both major parties include rich and poor) and state-level exceptions (e.g., California, Granger/Populist laws) when assessing real risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love of novelty / passion for destroying old institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracies are credited with loving novelty and destroying old institutions, but Americans, though fond of novelty in amusements and social life, are conservative about fundamental institutions of government and religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between frivolous appetite for novelty (amusements, literature) and conservatism about core institutions. Use this to judge whether a democracy seeks unnecessary institutional upheaval or preserves established political/religious structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability to be misled / influence of demagogues
rubrics_metrics.description: The inexperience of immigrants, lack of trained political thought among many citizens, and the sentimental tendencies of large masses make people open to fallacious reasoning and the persuasions of adventurers (demagogues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess susceptibility by examining presence and effect of demagogues (e.g., Granger and Populist movements). Note restraints on demagogues' harm in the U.S.: limited executive power over legislation, Senate consent for appointments, size and diversity of the country, and federal counterchecks that impede permanent mischief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laxity in enforcing unpopular laws / indulgence to offenders
rubrics_metrics.description: A disposition to be lax in enforcing laws disliked by any large part of the population, to tolerate breaches of public order, and to be too indulgent to offenders is one fault conspicuously manifested in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider causes cited (deficient reverence for law from popular government, easy-going national character, prejudice against maintaining police/military force, optimism about immigrants). Note that lax enforcement does not imply general lawlessness and may be replaced by firmness in crises; use as a test of enforcement rigor and public willingness to back enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commonness of mind and tone; lack of dignity in public affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy tends to produce a certain commonness of mind and tone and a want of dignity and elevation in the conduct of public affairs; public office is often not treated with heroic or elevated sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare expectations of public office dignity (noblesse oblige) with observed behavior: officials acting 'as one of the people', avoiding magnifying their office, or fearing to seem superior. Use this to judge the level of civic seriousness and the symbolic dignity attached to high office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apathy among the leisured and fastidious classes
rubrics_metrics.description: A consequence of democratic equality is a certain apathy among luxurious classes and fastidious minds, who feel of no more account than ordinary voters and are disgusted by superficial vulgarities of public life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the engagement of educated/leisured elites with public life; their withdrawal or apathy as a symptom of democratic leveling and its impact on governance quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Want of knowledge, tact, and judgment in legislation and administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy produces a want of knowledge, tact, and judgment in the details of legislation and administration, with inadequate recognition of the difficulty of these tasks and of the worth of special experience and skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as a metric to measure how well legislatures and administrations handle technical, complex policy matters and whether they defer appropriately to trained experts (economists, jurists, statesmen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Laxity in management of public business; susceptibility to corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons entrusted with public business being average men may not rise to a due sense of responsibility and may succumb to temptations presented by control of legislation and public funds; repression of such derelictions is often neglected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess incidence of corrupt appointments, jobs, tampering with elections, and whether political culture/accountability mechanisms check these abuses. Note examples of 'ringsters' and governors who committed jobs and tampered with elections then suffered electoral defeat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overconfidence of the masses leading to undervaluing delegated power and skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic self-confidence often passes into jealousy of delegated power and an undervaluing of skill and knowledge; the belief that any citizen is fit for any political work undermines selection for ability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure public attitudes toward experts and representative institutions; check whether popular theory pushes equality to extremes that degrade representation and specialized competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural defects of representative bodies (composition and separation)
rubrics_metrics.description: American legislatures are often disjoined from administrative offices; members are not selected for ability or experience but frequently represent local machines; the separation of executive from legislature affects the character of representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate composition and selection criteria of legislatures, the effect of separation of powers on administrative competence, and comparisons with other democracies (England, France) that may avoid these excesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incapacity to resolve intricate technical policy questions
rubrics_metrics.description: The masses can handle broad moral issues but are at fault on intricate questions requiring foresight, exact reasoning, or wide knowledge: currency and coinage, free trade vs. protection, constitutional/muncipal machinery reforms, control of corporations and Trusts, purity of elections, reform of criminal procedure, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a checklist of policy areas where democratic majorities historically struggle; examine past examples (Free Soil, Reconstruction) to judge performance and remaining evils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence of republican government on public virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Republics 'live by Virtue' — they require a high level of public spirit and justice among citizens; in very large, equal states one cannot expect citizens to rise above the average level of human nature without artificial helps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether civic virtue, personal dignity, patriotism, and willingness to accept sacrifices are present at levels sustaining the republic; consider whether institutional arrangements and traditions provide the 'artificial helps' (training, local self-government) that compensate for lack of elevated class-based leadership.
